name: Rafael Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Rafael. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the underground side, so less climbing, more holes. Our crew lays and joints cable for the new housing estates going up past the ring road, and we fix faults when a digger goes through a main. A jointing day is me in a pit with a tent over it, stripping back the sheath, fitting the joint, filling the resin, and it has to be perfect, because if it fails in five years somebody's street goes dark.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's careful work. Bernie, the old jointer who trained me, used to say a good joint is like a good weld, nobody sees it but everybody depends on it. What wears me out is kneeling. My knees are forty-three going on sixty, and in winter the pits fill with water faster than the pump can clear them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say now, that it's a useful tool and not much more. I use one of those chatbots now and then, I had it help me write a letter to the council about a parking fine. At work I'd probably shrug and say, good, back to digging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a little disappointed, because I thought it might take some of the dull paperwork off our plates. But for my family it changes nothing. Lucía keeps teaching, I keep jointing, we keep paying the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. We've got about nine months of savings and I'd keep adding to them. I'd keep using the chatbot for letters and maybe for checking a cable spec, the way I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, like a match that got called off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What paperwork were you hoping it would take off your plate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Permits, mostly. Every dig needs a traffic plan, a permit from the highways people, photos before and after. I spend Friday afternoons in the van with a clipboard. If a machine did that I'd have been happy, but I'd not cry over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody really, in that version. Maybe the office lads who do the permits, if the bit of automation it does manage lands on them. But mostly it's just life going on.

S0.say: I'd say AI turned out to be a handy tool and nothing more, like the chatbot I use for council letters, and at work I'd shrug and get back to digging.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed it didn't take more of the dull paperwork, but for my family nothing changes. My partner keeps teaching and I keep jointing cable.
S0.do: Carries on as he is and keeps adding to about nine months of savings. Keeps using a chatbot now and then for letters and for checking cable specifications.
S0.feel: Calm, a bit flat, like a match that got called off.
S0.quote: I spend Friday afternoons in the van with a clipboard. If a machine did that I'd have been happy, but I'd not cry over it.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael is relaxed and slightly let down that the hype didn't remove permit paperwork. He already uses AI occasionally for personal admin, which makes him neither a fan nor a refuser. Nothing in this picture threatens his household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to make sure the gains get shared. If the company saves money because AI plans the routes and drones survey the lines, some of that should go to wages and training, not just to the people at the top. I'd say that at the union meeting and to my brother-in-law, who thinks I'm a communist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think underground jointing is one of the last things they'd automate. It's wet, it's cramped, every pit is different. I think I'd see the planning side change, and maybe I'd get a tablet that tells me which joints are failing before they fail, which would actually be good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on whatever course they offer on the new fault-finding kit, once a couple of the others had tried it and said it works. I'd use the AI tools more for the permits if the company allows it. And I'd back the union pushing for a training fund written into the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little curious, actually. Bit of worry for the office staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said once a couple of others had tried it. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first version of anything is rubbish. They gave us a GPS cable locator three years ago that put the main two metres from where it was, and Jonno nearly went through a gas pipe. Now the second version is great. I'll wait for the second version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo's fourteen and he's already using AI for his homework more than he admits. I'd say to him, use it, but learn to do something with your hands too, because hands are harder to replace. Inés is ten, she'd just ask if robots are coming to school.

S1.say: I'd say the gains have to be shared, so if AI and drones save the company money, part of it should go to wages and training rather than just to the people at the top.
S1.think: Underground jointing would be one of the last jobs automated because every wet, cramped pit is different. The planning side would change, and fault-predicting tools could actually help me.
S1.do: Signs up for training on new fault-finding equipment once colleagues have tested it. Uses AI tools more for permits if allowed, and backs the union's push for a training fund in the next contract.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a little curious, with some worry for office staff.
S1.quote: They gave us a GPS cable locator three years ago that put the main two metres from where it was, and Jonno nearly went through a gas pipe.
S1.fieldNote: His caution is learned from a specific bad tool, not from fear of technology. He wants gains shared and backs union bargaining, but sounds personally secure. Advice to his son about hands-on skills shows how he thinks about safety from automation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the government to step in, big. Some kind of basic income, paid for by taxing the companies that own the machines. I'd be saying it everywhere, and for once I don't think my brother-in-law would argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. Two years isn't enough for a robot to get good in a flooded pit, I don't think, but I don't really know. And if every other job goes first, then every other worker wants mine, and the pay falls even if I keep it. Nine months of savings looks small when the whole country's in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the big things straight away: we were going to redo the kitchen next spring, that's off. I'd overpay the mortgage with what we'd saved for it. I'd join the union campaign for a basic income and go on the marches, and I'd talk to Lucía about what her school is planning, because teaching would get hit too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but there's a knot. I'd feel it every time I drove past the estate we're building and wondered who'll be able to afford those houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first, after the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car. We'd manage with one, I can get a lift to the depot with Jonno. Then the kids' extra clubs, but only once we had to, because that's the last thing I want them to feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the houses on the estate. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We're laying power to three hundred new homes. If people's jobs vanish in two years, who buys them? I'd be jointing cable to empty streets. That's the picture that gets me, not the robot in the pit.

S2.say: I'd say government has to step in big, with a basic income paid for by taxing the companies that own the machines, and I'd be saying it everywhere.
S2.think: It scares me, because even if robots can't handle flooded pits that fast, everyone else losing work would push down my pay. Nine months of savings looks small when the whole country is struggling.
S2.do: Cancels the kitchen renovation planned for next spring and puts that money on the mortgage. Joins the union's basic income campaign and marches, then sells the second car if needed.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a knot in his stomach, but not panicking.
S2.quote: We're laying power to three hundred new homes. If people's jobs vanish in two years, who buys them? I'd be jointing cable to empty streets.
S2.fieldNote: His fear is less about a robot taking his task than about the economy around him collapsing. He thinks in terms of the whole society and reaches straight for public policy. His cuts are ordered and calm, which fits his strong savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now. Training money, a plan for every region, rules on how fast companies can replace crews. I'd be pushing the union to get ahead of it instead of reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd come through it better than most. Five years is time to learn the robot side of the job, the person who sets up the machine in the pit and checks its work. I'd be forty-eight, my knees would thank me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Second year in, once I could see which robots were actually working, I'd sign up for the evening course at the technical college on cable diagnostics and remote equipment. Keep saving, finish the kitchen fund but leave it in the bank. And I'd put my name forward for the union's tech committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel like I had a hand on the wheel. That makes a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until the second year for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as with the locator. In year one there'll be ten companies selling robots and half of them will be junk. By year two you know which ones the utility's buying, and you learn that one. No point learning the wrong machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd leave the kitchen money in the bank. What's that money for, in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the we-don't-know money. Lucía calls it the rainy-day kitchen. If it all goes fine, we get a kitchen in 2032. If it doesn't, we've got another few months.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if we start now, with training money, regional plans and rules on how fast companies can replace crews.
S3.think: I'd come through it better than most, because five years is enough to learn to set up and check the robots in the pit. My knees would thank me.
S3.do: Waits a year to see which robots the utility actually buys, then takes an evening course in cable diagnostics and remote equipment. Keeps the kitchen fund in the bank and joins the union's technology committee.
S3.feel: Uneasy but with a hand on the wheel, which makes a big difference to him.
S3.quote: If it all goes fine, we get a kitchen in 2032. If it doesn't, we've got another few months.
S3.fieldNote: Five years flips him from defensive to planning. His wait-for-the-second-version habit shapes even his retraining timing. The rainy-day kitchen shows how the household keeps options open without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this fairly, and if we mess it up that's on the politicians. I'd want a proper national plan, like after the mines closed, but done right this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fairly relaxed about ten years. I'd be fifty-three, with Mateo out of school and Inés nearly there. I could ride the job a good while, learn the new side of it, and keep the house safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep jointing, take the diagnostics course around year three or four, and keep saving. I'd talk to Mateo seriously about what he studies, maybe steer him to something that designs or repairs the machines rather than something they'll replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the low background kind. More about the country than about us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the mines. Is that personal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandad worked in one. When it closed he got a pay-off and nothing else, and the town never recovered. If you give people ten years' warning and still do it like that, that's a choice, not an accident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look at what keeps the robots going. Somebody has to repair them, power them, make the rules for them. I'd want him in that, not in an office job a computer can do. But he's fourteen, he'll do what he wants.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to handle this fairly, with a proper national plan like after the mines closed, and if it goes wrong that's on politicians.
S4.think: I'm fairly relaxed about ten years, because I'd be fifty-three with the kids nearly through school. I could ride the job a good while and learn its new side.
S4.do: Keeps jointing and takes the diagnostics course in year three or four while continuing to save. Talks seriously with his son about studying something that repairs or designs machines.
S4.feel: A low background unease, more about the country than about his own family.
S4.quote: If you give people ten years' warning and still do it like that, that's a choice, not an accident.
S4.fieldNote: Family history from his grandfather's mine closure shapes how he judges the slow scenario. He feels personally safe with ten years and his concern turns outward to policy. His advice to his son is practical, and he admits he can't control it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. What would help is a basic income, or something like it, that kicks in before people lose the house, not after. And retraining that's paid, so you can feed your family while you learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the work means. A good joint is a bit of pride, you know? If I end up watching a robot do it, I'd want something else I can be proud of. Money's not the whole thing.

headlineQuote: A good joint is like a good weld, nobody sees it but everybody depends on it.
portrait: Rafael Garcia is a 43-year-old underground cable jointer laying power to new housing estates, married to Lucía, a primary teacher, with two children and about nine months of savings. He uses AI now and then for letters and waits for the second version of any new tool after a faulty cable locator nearly caused an accident. He's calm in the mild scenarios and pushes for shared gains through the union. Fast AGI makes him anxious mostly about a collapsing economy, while five or ten years let him plan to retrain into diagnostics and think about what his son should study.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because jobs across the country could vanish before anyone can adjust.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income that starts before people lose their homes, and paid retraining so families can eat while workers learn.
